problem.title: Card-fraud scoring service
problem.context: A payments company scores every card transaction for fraud before it is authorized. It processes about 3,000 transactions per second on a normal day and up to five times as many during seasonal sales. Fraudsters adapt within weeks, and the confirmed fraud labels (chargebacks) arrive days to weeks after the transaction. Auditors and the card schemes can ask, months later, why a given transaction was scored the way it was. The ML team has five data scientists and two ML engineers. The company's operations team runs the data centres and the shared infrastructure, but there is no platform team for machine learning.

requirements.text: Score every card transaction before the authorization decision, using the cardholder's recent activity (for example, the spending of the last hour and the last day).
Update the model as new confirmed fraud cases arrive.
For any past score, show which model version and which input values produced it.
During a seasonal peak of 15,000 transactions per second, a score comes back within 30 ms at the 99th percentile.
When the scoring service or one of its data sources fails, authorizations go on. The business accepts weaker fraud detection for up to 15 minutes, but no authorization may fail because of scoring.
An auditor asks about a score from up to 13 months ago. Within one working day the team answers with the model version, the input values and the training data that model was built from.
When the fraud loss rate rises in one segment, a retrained model can be in production within 48 hours, after it has been compared with the current model on recent transactions.
Card data must stay inside the company's PCI-certified environment: no external service may process it.
Seven people build and run the system, with no dedicated ML platform team.

points.description: This system uses MLOps to ingest and process streaming data in real time, store it in a shared data store, and provide features through general-purpose data stores. A scheduled automated pipeline performs batch model training, evaluation, and validation; one validated model is deployed as a model microservice for real-time predictions, with data and predictions monitored and models manually adjusted and redeployed.

A continuous data stream is ingested and processed in real time, with features persisted in general-purpose data stores without specialized feature-store support. Each model runs as its own service, while model-serving microservices access the relevant features and deliver predictions or scores in real time.

The system ingests data in batches, processes it in batch-oriented workflows, and stores features in general-purpose data stores without specialized feature-store support. Each model runs as its own service, while scheduled batch jobs invoke the service to generate predictions or scores and write the results back to data storage.

The system uses MLOps with a data-version repository and scheduled pipeline runs. Each run performs batch model training, evaluation, and validation automatically, while monitoring-driven model changes are reviewed, adjusted, and redeployed manually.

An MLOps system versions data in a technology-supported repository and triggers an automated model-building pipeline when new training data becomes available. The pipeline incrementally trains, evaluates, and validates models, while automated measures adjust them based on monitoring results.

The system stores machine-learning data in a shared data store and tracks its versions in a dedicated data-version repository. In production, it logs and monitors system data and model predictions, complementing the repository’s data-versioning function with operational monitoring.

The system obtains machine-learning data manually or through event streaming without retaining it in a data store. It does not version the data or monitor and track the model in production, so operation is possible but reproducibility, historical comparison, and production visibility are limited.

trajectory.hypothesis: The mapped solution decisions form a coherent design point for real-time scoring, historical reconstruction and controlled retraining.
trajectory.observation: The mapped values describe the streaming scorer and scheduled model lifecycle. The point has no warnings or unmet required dimensions, but no source attests this combination. The solution directly describes safe rule-engine fallback and PCI-contained operation, which the selected dimensions do not model. It does not satisfy the 48-hour production target because the shadow comparison lasts three days. The latency target is plausible from the architecture but has no stated load-test result.

trajectory.hypothesis: R1 and Q1 explain a continuous transaction stream, up-to-date per-card features, and synchronous real-time service scoring.
trajectory.observation: The region fits the before-authorization scoring path and recent-activity features. Its design-space values are accepted but have no passages or attesting sources in this workspace, and the solution gives no measured 15,000 TPS/30 ms result; the latency claim remains only partly established.

trajectory.hypothesis: The real-time values are needed for R1 and Q1; compare a batch-oriented alternative to see whether those requirements force the online path.
trajectory.observation: This rival changes three related choices together: batch ingestion, batch processing and batch scoring. It cannot return a score for each transaction before authorization or meet the stated latency scenario. This is a workflow contrast, not an option the solution says it considered; it supports the need for an online path, while the particular service and datastore choices remain less constrained.

trajectory.hypothesis: R2 and Q3 explain repeatable scheduled batch retraining, recorded training inputs, and a reviewable human promotion decision.
trajectory.observation: Nightly pipeline retraining on labelled transactions addresses model updates, and the recorded snapshot, artifact and model version support reconstruction. Human review fits the team's oversight but the three-day shadow period misses the 48-hour production limit. The automation reduces routine work, though the solution does not show the operating effort required of seven people. The workspace has no passages attesting the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: A data-arrival-triggered incremental and automatic retraining path might better explain Q4 than the solution's scheduled batch and human-gated path.
trajectory.observation: This rival workflow could react sooner to new labels, but automatic adjustment would remove the risk team's stated manual comparison and promotion gate. Since the three-day shadow comparison is still required by Q4 and the solution's promotion policy exceeds 48 hours, incremental learning alone does not establish the deadline. The chosen batch schedule and human gate are not forced by R2; they are design choices within the stated update requirement.

trajectory.hypothesis: R3 and Q3 explain durable score/input logs plus versioned training data and model records.
trajectory.observation: The 13-month append-only score records preserve model versions and input values, while the MLflow run snapshot connects a model artifact to its training data. The chosen values fit shared persistence, data versioning and production logging. No source passages attest this combination in the workspace.

trajectory.hypothesis: Q3 should require retained, versioned and logged records; compare a no-persistence/no-tracking region to see whether those choices are forced.
trajectory.observation: Without a data store, training-data versioning or production tracking, the team cannot reconstruct a score and its training data months later. The audit requirement therefore forces retained records and some form of versioning/tracking, though it does not force the particular object store or MLflow technology. This changes several related choices as a grouped auditability contrast.

regions.name: Online transaction scoring
regions.reason: R1 requires a fresh score from recent activity before each authorization, and Q1 makes this an online path. The space's descriptions fit that path, while this run has no source passages to attest it and no performance measurement to establish Q1 fully.

regions.name: Historical score reconstruction
regions.reason: R3 and Q3 call for retaining scores, model versions, input values and training snapshots. These values represent shared storage, data versioning and production logging; the exact retention and append-only implementation come from the solution.

alternatives.name: Fraud scoring as built
alternatives.summary: A PCI-contained streaming scorer uses per-card Redis aggregates and a synchronous model service with a rule-engine fallback. Nightly batch retraining is tracked in MLflow, compared in shadow mode, and promoted manually; historical scores and inputs are retained for audit.

choices.reason: A separate model service fits the synchronous transaction path, but a monolith or local service could also expose an online score; the requirements do not force this deployment boundary.
choices.solution_quote: The model is a gradient-boosted tree model (XGBoost). It is packaged in a container with a small Python REST service and runs on the company's Kubernetes cluster, with six replicas and autoscaling on CPU.

choices.reason: Redis holds the current feature aggregates without a feature-store-specific layer, which fits this value. The requirements need timely feature access but do not require a general-purpose store over a feature store.
choices.solution_quote: Flink jobs consume the topic and keep per-card aggregates (spend and counts over the last hour, day and week, and the number of distinct merchants) up to date in a Redis cluster.

choices.reason: A synchronous, real-time service returns the score before authorization; batch scoring would miss R1 and Q1. The particular microservice form is a reasonable implementation choice within that forced online requirement.
choices.solution_quote: The authorization switch calls the service synchronously with a 25 ms timeout.

choices.reason: A continuous stream is consistent with scoring every transaction and maintaining its recent activity as it arrives.
choices.solution_quote: The payments switch publishes every card transaction to a Kafka topic inside the PCI-certified environment.

choices.reason: Per-card aggregates must be current for each online score, so real-time processing is called for by R1 and Q1.
choices.solution_quote: Flink jobs consume the topic and keep per-card aggregates (spend and counts over the last hour, day and week, and the number of distinct merchants) up to date in a Redis cluster.

choices.reason: The promoted model is the active production model and its version is logged with each score. The space does not represent the details of running a candidate in shadow without serving it to authorization traffic.
choices.solution_quote: The scoring service loads the promoted model at its next restart.

choices.reason: Historical reconstruction requires durable score and input storage. The requirement forces persistence, while the on-premises object store is the solution's choice of shared store.
choices.solution_quote: Every score is written, with the model version and all input values, to an append-only table in the company's on-premises object store, kept for 13 months.

choices.reason: Q3 requires the training data behind an older model to be recoverable; MLflow's saved training snapshot is a data-version repository fit. The exact registry product is not forced.
choices.solution_quote: MLflow records the parameters, the metrics, the training data snapshot and the model artifact of every run, and holds the model registry.

choices.reason: A nightly schedule updates from delayed labels, but R2 does not specify a schedule; event-driven or on-demand retraining could also update the model.
choices.solution_quote: An Airflow pipeline retrains the model every night on the last 90 days of labelled transactions.

choices.reason: An automated model-building pipeline supports repeated retraining and comparison, but the requirements do not force Airflow or this pipeline form.
choices.solution_quote: An Airflow pipeline retrains the model every night on the last 90 days of labelled transactions.

choices.reason: The solution uses offline batch training over labelled history. R2 requires updates when labels arrive but does not require batch learning over incremental learning.
choices.solution_quote: An Airflow pipeline retrains the model every night on the last 90 days of labelled transactions.

choices.reason: The score and its inputs must be logged to answer historical questions. The solution also monitors distributions, but this value only approximately captures the additional drift dashboards and alerts.
choices.solution_quote: Every score is written, with the model version and all input values, to an append-only table in the company's on-premises object store, kept for 13 months.
choices.fit_note: The value captures production logging of data and predictions; it does not specifically express score-distribution drift monitoring, alerting, or the three-feature explanations returned to the dispute team.

choices.reason: Human review and promotion provide a governance gate, but Q4 calls for comparison rather than manual adjustment specifically. The choice is free and contributes to the three-day delay that conflicts with Q4.
choices.solution_quote: The risk team reviews the comparison and promotes it by hand in MLflow.

choices.reason: A managed ML lifecycle supports repeatable retraining, lineage and registry operations for a small team. The constraint does not force MLOps, but the solution chooses it to make those tasks repeatable.
choices.solution_quote: An Airflow pipeline retrains the model every night on the last 90 days of labelled transactions. MLflow records the parameters, the metrics, the training data snapshot and the model artifact of every run, and holds the model registry.

adrs.title: Keep transaction features current and score online
adrs.context: Each transaction needs a score before authorization using recent per-card behavior, with a 30 ms p99 target at peak load. The solution uses a continuous transaction stream, real-time feature aggregation, Redis, and a synchronous model service.

options.name: Streaming features and online model service
pros: Matches per-transaction scoring and recently updated activity features.
cons: The design provides no measured evidence for the 15,000 TPS and 30 ms p99 target; service, container, autoscaling and fallback details are outside these values.
options.reason: The online path is required by R1 and the latency objective; using a per-model microservice and Redis is a free implementation choice. The workspace has no source passages attesting this combination.

options.name: Batch ingestion, processing and scoring
pros: Batch workflows can process groups of data on a schedule.
cons: Would not supply a fresh score before authorization or meet the 30 ms response objective.
options.reason: This grouped workflow contrast misses R1 and Q1. These values are alternatives supplied by the space, not alternatives the solution says it considered.

adrs.title: Retain enough lineage to reconstruct historical scores
adrs.context: A score must remain explainable for 13 months: the team needs its exact model version and inputs as well as the training data snapshot behind that model.

options.name: Durable score records, data versioning and production logs
pros: Preserves score inputs and model version, and connects trained artifacts to a recorded data snapshot.
cons: The exact 13-month append-only retention policy and one-working-day retrieval process are not represented by the values.
options.reason: R3 and Q3 force durable logging and recoverable training-data lineage. The shared object store and MLflow implementation are free choices; this combination is not attested by sources in the workspace.

options.name: No persistent store, data versioning or production tracking
pros: Avoids maintaining historical storage and tracking.
cons: Cannot reproduce old scores or identify their model inputs and training data.
options.reason: This rival misses R3 and Q3. The space offers it as a contrast, but the solution does not say the team considered it.

adrs.title: Automate retraining and retain a human promotion gate
adrs.context: Confirmed fraud labels arrive with delay, so the model needs recurring updates and the small team needs a repeatable process to train, record, compare and promote versions. The solution runs nightly batch retraining and keeps promotion under risk-team review.

options.name: Scheduled batch training with manual review and promotion
pros: Updates from accumulated confirmed labels and records each run; the risk team can review a candidate before promotion.
cons: The three-day shadow period exceeds Q4's 48-hour production limit, and the solution does not quantify the operating load on seven people.
options.reason: R2 supports recurring batch retraining and C2 makes automation useful, but neither forces the nightly schedule, batch learning, MLOps tools or manual gate. The human comparison is retained by choice and its three-day duration trades off Q4.

options.name: Data-arrival-triggered incremental and automated adjustment
pros: Could respond quickly as new training data arrives.
cons: Automatic adjustment removes the solution's risk-team promotion gate and does not alone ensure a 48-hour comparison-and-release cycle.
options.reason: This rival is a grouped workflow contrast and is not stated as considered by the solution. It may shorten training latency but does not resolve the release deadline on its own.

uncovered.decision: Keeping card data and all services inside the PCI-certified environment
uncovered.solution_quote: The payments switch publishes every card transaction to a Kafka topic inside the PCI-certified environment.

uncovered.decision: Fallback to the rule engine when scoring or a data source fails
uncovered.solution_quote: If the call times out or fails, the switch uses the existing rule engine for that transaction and logs that no score was used.

uncovered.decision: Container, Kubernetes replicas and CPU autoscaling for serving capacity
uncovered.solution_quote: It is packaged in a container with a small Python REST service and runs on the company's Kubernetes cluster, with six replicas and autoscaling on CPU.

uncovered.decision: Use XGBoost and return top contributing features for dispute explanations
uncovered.solution_quote: The model is a gradient-boosted tree model (XGBoost).

uncovered.decision: Run a candidate model in shadow mode for three days before manual promotion
uncovered.solution_quote: A new model first runs in shadow mode next to the production model for three days; the risk team reviews the comparison and promotes it by hand in MLflow.

uncovered.decision: Alert on score-distribution drift from last month
uncovered.solution_quote: Grafana dashboards show the score distribution and the share of rule-engine fallbacks, and alert when the score distribution drifts from last month's.

unaddressed.note: The solution does provide rule-engine fallback, but the space has no decision about failure handling or graceful degradation, so this requirement cannot be evaluated through a design-space region.
The requirement allows production within 48 hours after comparison, while the candidate runs in shadow for three days before manual promotion.
The solution keeps data and services in the PCI-certified environment, but the space has no security boundary or deployment-location decision to represent that constraint.
